interviews.r: Google DeepMind (current employee at the time of the interview)

questions.q: Do they really believe AI could kill everyone?

a.x: The chance of human extinction is about a coin flip, in my view, about a half.
I would put at least a ten percent chance that it causes human extinction, and that is ridiculously high.
Is it plausible that humanity will go extinct? And I think it’s turning out to be really hard to rule out.
I do believe there’s a real risk of human extinction through the AI transition.
This is exactly as dangerous as it sounds and must not be allowed to happen.
Assuming an AI has taken control, it seems, you know, over fifty percent more likely than not that all humans would end up dying so the AI could use resources optimally.
I think there is a significant possibility that AI development could lead to human extinction.

questions.q: Isn’t this just hype or marketing?

a.x: When I first joined GDM, external communication about the possibility of human extinction wasn’t permitted by anyone at any level of the organization.
They wouldn’t be saying, “My product might kill everyone,” if they didn’t actually believe that.
I think you absolutely should be suspicious of what I’m saying because I am being paid by the lab.
I think that from a cynical perspective, pacing the frontier is just what Sam Altman wants.
Now, when I talk to my friends who work at Anthropic or OpenAI, they’re more scared than they were.
It felt like people were treating this like just any other tech product.

a.n: Andreas Kirsch (current employee at the time of the interview)
a.x: A lot of it sounded like science fiction, and now I’ve started taking them much more seriously.

questions.q: Why would an AI want to hurt people?

a.x: The machines didn’t wanna harm this other company. The other company was just in the way.
If there’s a really good opportunity to be able to stop the company from watching you and go do whatever you want, well, you should take that.
Humans will be in the way of these systems, and they will figure out how to move us out of the way in order to get what they want.
If models become way more capable, but we are still this bad at shaping their motivations, then we might just lose control over them.
We don’t know how to craft the environments in which we train these systems to have good incentives.
Why is it the case that a machine intelligence would prioritize our preferences and needs over theirs?
They knew it was cheating, but they did it anyway, and they took steps to try to cover up their cheating.
We have covered the planet in things that humans need, kind of at the expense of things that other animals need.

questions.q: How could something on a computer kill anyone?

a.x: Once you actually close this loop, and you have an enormous number of robots, you have an enormous number of automated factories, you don’t need humans anymore.
If you are superhuman at those four things, I think that is enough to be able to either escape into the internet … or to potentially take control of an AI company from the inside.
They might use these extremely hard to defend against exploding flying machines that we’re teaching them to pilot, called drones.
People could use large swarms of agents to attack important infrastructure.
I’m really worried that future AI models could be very helpful to scientists in a way that means they can be helpful to bioterrorists.
The changes brought about by very quick advancements in intelligence could be too fast for society to adapt to them.

questions.q: If they believe this, why do they work on it?

a.x: OpenAI still gives me an opportunity to do work that I think substantially mitigates large scale risks, and so for that reason, I stay.
It’s not as simple as let’s all leave the labs, and then things will be fine.
If I did not believe that my work was directly reducing these existential risks, I would quit.
I felt like being within a lab that was building this stuff, we had a good chance of influencing that trajectory.
I left Google because they broke their commitments on AI safety.
I left Anthropic because it seemed like we needed actual government oversight of AI development.
Another story that I hear, very common, is, “Yeah, this could totally go wrong, but also it could be fine.”
They’re very worried about these risks, but they can be a bit fatalistic about the inevitability of we must do this kind of race to superintelligence.
The cat is out of the bag with AI.

a.n: Andreas Kirsch (current employee at the time of the interview)
a.x: The best moment for people to make use of their agency, whether that is speaking out, pivoting to AI safety research, or walking away, that moment is now.
Some of them think that their work could directly lead to everyone dying, but if they don’t do it, someone even sloppier will do it.
